research_text:
# Research brief: `javax.crypto.Cipher` and the CipherSpec finding

**Source limits (read first):**
- The search tool returned excerpts of pages, not full documents. The excerpts of Cipher.crysl came from the GitHub blob view, not the raw URL you gave.
- I pieced the rule text together from several excerpts of the same file. They do not cover all 139 lines, so I flag where something may be missing.
- Nothing in the sources explains your exact detector message, and I did not look at any repository.

## Q1. What `Cipher` governs, and what the finding refers to

**What `Cipher` governs**
- The Java 8 Javadoc says Cipher "forms the core of the Java Cryptographic Extension (JCE) framework". See https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/javax/crypto/Cipher.html. Its `getInstance` takes a transformation name and returns a Cipher implementing it.
- The `init` overloads initialize the cipher with a key. Optional arguments are algorithm parameters (`AlgorithmParameterSpec` or `AlgorithmParameters`) and a `SecureRandom`. A `Certificate` overload also exists. See https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/Cipher.html.
- The Java 25 Javadoc says that initializing a Cipher loses all previously acquired state. Initializing is equivalent to creating and initializing a new instance. See https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/Cipher.html.

**What the finding refers to**
- The finding concerns the `key` argument of an `init` event.
- In the CrySL rule, that argument is the `java.security.Key key` object. It is the second argument in `init(encmode, key, ...)`.
- The rule's `REQUIRES` block says that key must carry a `generatedKey`, `generatedPubkey` or `generatedPrivkey` predicate. In CrySL, such a predicate is granted to an object another rule's `ENSURES` block covers, when that object is used correctly. See https://eclipse.dev/cognicrypt/documentation/crysl/.
- The CryptoAnalysis README calls this kind of error a `RequiredPredicateError`. It describes the case as an object expecting another object to have been used correctly. A Cipher requiring a correctly generated key is its example. See https://github.com/themaplelab/CryptoAnalysis.
- A paper on dependent errors (https://www.bodden.de/pubs/wsv+23supporting.pdf) describes a "specified object" that requires a predicate from an "ensuring object". If the ensuring object is itself misused, the predicate is not ensured and a RequiredPredicateError follows.
- The same paper describes dependent error trees linking such errors. That is the closest documented concept to "already reported by the specification that produced it".

**Unresolved**
- No source defines your exact message text.
- "UnsatisfiedConstraint" is not among the error names I found. The names found were ConstraintError, ForbiddenMethodError, ImpreciseValueExtractionError, IncompleteOperationError, NeverTypeOfError, RequiredPredicateError, TypestateError and HardCodedError. I could not map it to any of them.
- Whether the message means the finding is a deduplicated, dependent report is my reading of the dependent-error-tree concept. The sources do not confirm it.

## Q2. Documented correct and safe usage, and the remediation it gives

**Transformation**
- The Java 26 Javadoc recommends a transformation that fully specifies algorithm, mode and padding. A bare algorithm name falls back to provider-specific defaults. See https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/Cipher.html.
- The JCA Reference Guide says SunJCE and SunPKCS11 default to ECB mode and PKCS5Padding for many symmetric ciphers. See https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/technotes/guides/security/crypto/CryptoSpec.html.

**Initialization and parameters**
- If a cipher needs parameters that cannot be derived from the key, the provider generates them itself (provider defaults or random values) when encrypting or wrapping. It raises an exception when decrypting or unwrapping. See the Java 8 Javadoc above.
- The same parameters used for encryption must be used for decryption. They can be read with `getParameters()` or `getIV()`. See the JCA guide above.

**GCM and nonce lifecycle (Javadoc, Java 8 and later)**
- The Javadoc says GCM has a uniqueness requirement on IVs used for encryption with a given key. Repeated IVs make the usage subject to forgery attacks.
- It says callers should re-initialize the cipher with GCM parameters carrying a different IV after each GCM encryption operation. See https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/javax/crypto/Cipher.html.
- The JCA Reference Guide says callers should not reuse key and IV combinations for GCM encryption. See https://docs.oracle.com/javase/9/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.htm.
- `doFinal` resets the cipher to its state at the previous `init`. This is why the Javadoc tells callers to re-initialize with a new IV.

**AAD and authentication**
- For GCM and CCM, all AAD must be supplied through `updateAAD` before `update` or `doFinal` processes the ciphertext. `updateAAD` is marked since 1.7. See https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/Cipher.html.
- In AEAD modes, the authentication tag is appended on encryption and verified on decryption. See the same page.

**Key provenance**
- I found no official statement in the Javadoc or the JCA guide for the exact CrySL concept of a key produced by a "specification that produced it". The `KeyGenerator` and `generatedKey` link is defined by CrySL, not by the JCA. See https://eclipse.dev/cognicrypt/documentation/crysl/ and https://bodden.de/pubs/ksa+18crysl.pdf.
- The Javadoc's `init` text says only that a key can be rejected as inappropriate for the cipher, or when it needs parameters that cannot be determined from it. See https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/Cipher.html.

**Remediation**
- The official Cipher and JCA sources give no remediation text for a CrySL finding. They document only the usage guidance above.
- The CogniCrypt documentation describes a Required Predicate Error as one reported when the combination of several objects is used incorrectly. See https://eclipse.dev/cognicrypt/documentation/codeanalysis/.
- I did not find an official sentence on constant keys, IVs or nonces in the JCA material I retrieved. Your policy rule against constants is therefore not backed by an official Cipher source I retrieved.

## Q3. Compatibility documentation

**Persisted and wire formats**
- The JCA documentation does not define a persisted or wire format for Cipher output.
- Documented facts that bear on formats:
  - The GCM/CCM tag is appended to the ciphertext.
  - Decryption needs the same parameters (IV, GCM tag length, and so on) used for encryption.
  - Parameters can be exported with `AlgorithmParameters.getEncoded()`.
- Implications for migration, which the sources do not state outright:
  - Changing the transformation, IV or tag length changes what readers must supply.
  - A bare `"AES"` uses provider defaults, which the Javadoc says vary by provider.
- I found no documented migration path from old ciphertext formats to new ones.

**Platform and version support**
- `updateAAD` and `GCMParameterSpec` are marked since 1.7. See https://docs.oracle.com/javase/7/docs/api/javax/crypto/spec/GCMParameterSpec.html.
- `AES/GCM/NoPadding (128)` appears in the Java 11 and Java 25 "Security Algorithm Implementation Requirements". The Java 8 StandardNames excerpt I saw did not list it. Treat Java 8 GCM support as unverified from these excerpts. See https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html and https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/technotes/guides/security/StandardNames.html.
- JEP 329 describes ChaCha20-Poly1305 and says the nonce is supplied through `IvParameterSpec`. It adds that, with no spec, the nonce is randomly generated and obtainable via `getIV()`. See https://openjdk.org/jeps/329. The excerpt did not show the release number. It is not stated in my excerpts.
- The JDK implementation uses the `jdk.crypto.disabledAlgorithms` security property to decide whether an algorithm is allowed. See the Java 26 Javadoc above.
- The CrySL rule's allow-list is narrower than the JCA. It permits AES only in GCM, CTR, CTS, CFB or OFB with `NoPadding`, plus RSA and a few PBE algorithms. See the Q4 excerpts below. The rule is not a compatibility statement for the JCA.

## Q4. What Cipher.crysl itself states

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/Cipher.crysl. I read it through the GitHub blob view, https://github.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/blob/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/Cipher.crysl.

**Receiver type.** The rule opens with `SPEC javax.crypto.Cipher`. The CrySL documentation says the `SPEC` clause names the fully qualified class the rule applies to. The `EVENTS` block lists API calls that can be made on each Cipher object. See https://eclipse.dev/cognicrypt/documentation/crysl/.

**Method names and parameter lists.** Every event is a method name plus an explicit parameter list. The parameters are variables declared in `OBJECTS`. Verbatim, from the excerpts I could assemble:
```
i1: init(encmode, certificate);
```
